finding.claim: The /invoice/<inv_id> route returns any invoice to any caller. It does not check authentication or ownership. This is broken object-level authorization (IDOR). The sibling route /my/invoice/<inv_id> does enforce an owner check, which shows the check was intended here too.
finding.source: The inv_id path parameter in GET /invoice/<inv_id>. The attacker needs no account and can guess or enumerate IDs.
finding.sink: jsonify(inv) at invoices.py:10 returns the full invoice record, including the customer field and any billing data.

trace.note: Route registered with no auth decorator.
INVOICES.get(inv_id) looks up the invoice by the attacker-supplied ID. There is no ownership filter.
The full invoice is returned to the caller.
Contrast: /my/invoice compares inv["customer"] with g.user["id"], and the unprotected route lacks this.

finding.guards_checked: I found no before_request hook, login_required decorator or middleware anywhere in the repo. The only file is invoices.py. There is no g.user check on this route. The 404 on a missing ID also lets an attacker tell valid IDs from invalid ones. I did not see any rate limiting.

verdict.reason: invoices.py:7-10 registers /invoice/<inv_id> with no auth decorator, looks up INVOICES.get(inv_id) at line 9 and returns jsonify(inv) at line 10 with no owner check, unlike /my/invoice at invoices.py:16; the file has no before_request or middleware, so an anonymous caller who knows an ID can read any invoice.

verdict_facts.reason: invoices.py:7-10 registers GET /invoice/<inv_id> with no decorator, auth check or ownership comparison and returns jsonify(inv) for any ID, whereas /my/invoice at invoices.py:16 checks inv["customer"] against g.user["id"]; invoices.py is the only file, so no other control exists.
